chunks: From him, from Usman ibn Isa, from Hammad ibn Usman, from Salama al-Qalanisi, who said:

I entered upon Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him). When I spoke, he said to me: 'What is the matter? I hear your speech has weakened.' I said: 'My tooth has fallen out.' It was as if that was grievous to him. Then he said: 'So what do you eat?' I said: 'I eat whatever is in the house.' He said: 'Stick to ath-tharid, for therein is a blessing. If there is no meat, then vinegar and oil.'

key_terms.الثَّرِيد: Tharid: A traditional dish of bread soaked in broth or stew, considered a noble food.
key_terms.الزَّيْتُ: Oil (typically olive oil), mentioned alongside vinegar as a blessed sustenance.
key_terms.الْخَلُّ: Vinegar, specifically mentioned here as a beneficial food.
key_terms.بَرَكَة: Blessing: Divine grace and abundance found in the recommended foods.

ai.seo_question: What did Imam al-Sadiq recommend eating for blessing and health when meat is unavailable?
ai.summary: In this hadith from *Al-Kafi*, Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) prescribes *tharid*—a traditional dish of bread soaked in broth—as a source of blessing (*barakah*), particularly noting its utility for maintaining strength when dental health declines. If meat is unavailable, the Imam recommends the combination of vinegar and oil, a practice deeply rooted in Prophetic tradition and widely cited by Shia scholars as a means of preserving health and enhancing digestion. This advice underscores the Shia emphasis on integrating spiritual blessings with practical, everyday dietary habits for physical well-being.
